tagline: Cloud business phone and call center software: numbers, IVR, call routing, recordings, agent dashboards.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: The software layer here is the easy part: a call log, a routing tree, a recording player, some agent stats. The hard part is being a telephony provider, which means phone numbers, carrier interconnects, PSTN termination, emergency calling rules, recording consent law, and per-country registration paperwork. An agent can absolutely build you a softphone and a call database in an afternoon, but it will sit on top of somebody else's carrier account, which means you replaced a vendor with a different vendor plus your own on-call rotation. If your team is one or two people, a cheap number and a rented SIP trunk genuinely is the answer. If it is a real support queue where dropped calls cost money, voice quality and uptime are the product and you are not going to out-engineer that in a weekend.
coreLoopDIY: A self-hosted softphone plus call log: place and receive calls through a rented SIP or Twilio number, record them, transcribe them, and store notes against a contact.
requirements: A telephony provider account (Twilio, Telnyx, or a SIP trunk) with a purchased number
A publicly reachable HTTPS host for webhooks
A transcription API key if you want searchable calls
Willingness to read your local call recording consent rules
whatYouLose: Carrier redundancy and voice quality engineering, the thing you are actually paying for
IVR, skills based routing and queue overflow logic that has been debugged by other people's angry callers
Supervisor tooling: live queue monitoring, barge-in, whisper coaching, wallboards
Compliance scaffolding: emergency address registration, number porting, regional caller ID rules, retention policies
Mobile apps and desk phone provisioning, so agents are stuck at a browser tab
moatNotes: Anyone can write a call log. Almost nobody wants to be the entity legally responsible for a call that fails.
whyPeopleStillPay: Because voice is the one channel where degradation is immediately obvious and immediately expensive. A chat widget that lags is annoying; a call that drops mid-complaint costs a customer. Paying a telephony vendor buys carrier relationships, redundant media paths, number inventory across countries, and someone to escalate to at 2am when audio goes one way. The dashboard is just the receipt.
notes: The dashboard is a weekend, the dial tone is not. The moat is carrier interconnects, number inventory and the regulatory paperwork that comes with being the party responsible when a call fails.
prompt:
Build a self-hosted single-team phone console: place and receive real calls, log every one, and keep notes per contact.

Stack, no substitutions:
- Node 22 with Fastify for the server
- SQLite via better-sqlite3, file at ./data/calls.db
- Server rendered HTML with plain EJS templates and a little vanilla JS, no React
- Twilio Programmable Voice as the carrier layer, using the Twilio Voice JS SDK in the browser for the softphone

In scope:
- .env holds TWILIO_ACCOUNT_SID, TWILIO_AUTH_TOKEN, TWILIO_API_KEY, TWILIO_API_SECRET, TWILIO_TWIML_APP_SID, TWILIO_NUMBER, PUBLIC_BASE_URL, OPENAI_API_KEY. Never hardcode. Provide .env.example.
- GET /token issues a short lived Twilio Voice access token for the browser client
- POST /voice/outbound returns TwiML dialing the requested number from TWILIO_NUMBER
- POST /voice/inbound returns TwiML that rings the browser client, falls back to voicemail after 20 seconds
- Enable dual channel recording on both directions, store the recording URL and duration on the call row
- POST /voice/status and POST /voice/recording webhooks update the call row; validate the Twilio signature on every webhook
- Contacts table: name, e164 number, notes. Calls table: direction, from, to, contact_id, started_at, duration, status, recording_url, transcript, agent_note
- Web UI: one page with a dialpad and a live call state banner, a call history table with inline playback and an editable note field, and a contacts page
- Background job that pulls finished recordings and transcribes them with the OpenAI transcription API, saved to calls.transcript
- Full text search across transcripts and notes using SQLite FTS5
- A visible banner on the dial screen reading "Recording is on. Announce it." because consent law is your problem now
- README covering: buying a number, creating the TwiML app, pointing it at PUBLIC_BASE_URL, and running with ngrok for local testing

Out of scope, do not build:
- Multi tenant accounts, billing, user signup. Single shared HTTP basic auth password from .env is enough
- IVR trees, skills based routing, queues, supervisor barge-in
- Number porting, emergency address handling, SMS
- Any telemetry or analytics calls to third parties

Deliver: package.json with a single npm start, migrations that run on boot, seed script that inserts two fake contacts, and a smoke test that stubs the Twilio webhooks and asserts a call row is created, updated and searchable.
